Les voix du décrochage scolaire : Partir: Voices of School Dropouts: Leaving Without a Diploma, Staying Without a Future?
Chaque année, des centaines de jeunes qu: Every year, hundreds of young people leave school without a diploma, pushed out by a system that seems to have forgotten them.
Cyril Guiot, l’intervenant Volet scolair: Cyril Guiot, school component outreach worker for Revdec’s Long-Term Program, and Nassera Éloire, coordinator of Rev Dec.
<strong>Cet article a été proposé et réd: This article was pitched and written by Aya, one of the students in the 2024-2025 cohort of École Converse. This year, the program welcomed Aya as well as Aude, Sabrina, Firas, Cindy and Sènan. Over five months, we taught them the basics of journalism. We are publishing a short series of three of their articles, and this is the first.
Pour cet article, je me suis intéressée: For this article, I looked into a phenomenon that still affects too many young people in Montréal: dropping out of school. It’s a subject we often hear discussed through statistics, but much less through the stories of young people who have left school or of those working to bring them back.
Je suis donc allée à la rencontre de jeu: So I went to meet young people who quit school or almost did, as well as a worker and a manager at Revdec, a community organization that supports young dropouts every day. They opened their doors to me and told me stories that were sometimes hard, but often inspiring.
Ce travail est aussi le fruit de plusieu: This piece is also the result of several interviews with young people from a range of backgrounds, who agreed to share their journeys, their doubts and their hopes. I thank them for that. For me, it was essential that their voices be at the heart of this article.
Merci aussi aux membres de Revdec pour l: Thank you also to the members of Revdec for their generosity and the time they gave me.
J’espère que ce texte contribuera à mieu: I hope this text will help people better understand the realities behind the word “dropout” and let us hear those we listen to far too little.
<strong>À Montréal, dans certains quarti: In Montréal, in some neighbourhoods, one student in five leaves school before earning a diploma. Behind that figure are faces and stories that often go unseen. La Converse met four young people who have experienced dropping out or nearly gave in to it. Their stories cross paths within the walls of an adult school in Hochelaga and at the tables of a McDonald’s. They tell us what pushed them out the door and what might, perhaps, make them stay.
<strong>19 h 37. </strong>L’enseigne jau: 7:37 p.m. The yellow sign of the Côte-des-Neiges McDonald’s lights up the slippery sidewalk. It’s March, and at this hour the dining room of the fast-food restaurant is still full: students, tired workers and a few regulars who seem to know the place like the back of their hand. In one corner, three young people are laughing loudly. In front of them, empty trays and half-finished cups of soda. They look like they know each other well.
Je m’approche avec mon café et me présen: I walk over with my coffee and introduce myself. They size me up for a moment, then one of them, Malik, invites me to sit down. He’s 19, Joey is 20 and Hana is 17. None of them is in school.
« J’ai arrêté en secondaire quatre, comm: “I stopped in Secondary 4,” Malik begins, shrugging. “I was trying to hang on, but it was just too much. I was helping my mom with my little brothers, and when I got back to class, I was wiped out. I wasn’t listening to anything. And on top of that, the teachers looked at me like I was already done for. At some point, I just decided to stop going.”
We talk about what pushed them out. Lack of support, racism, poverty. “It’s weird, right? They always tell us we have to work harder, that we have to prove we deserve our place,” says Hana. “But even when we do that, it’s never enough.”
Joey regarde son téléphone et tapote ner: Joey looks at his phone and taps nervously on the table: “There are schools where it feels like they’re just waiting for us to leave.”
<strong>« Mon fils n’est pas un cas perd: “My son is not a lost cause”
Une femme s’approche de notre table. Ell: A woman comes up to our table. She overheard the conversation and asks if she can talk to us. Her name is Fatou. She is in her forties, and her son dropped out last year. “I did everything I could,” she says, clasping her hands. “I pushed him, I encouraged him. But every day he came home and told me he didn’t feel included. That the teachers only saw his mistakes. He ended up believing he was a failure before he even had a chance.”
Quelques rides se dessinent sur son visa: A few lines are etched on her face, signs of weariness and life’s hardships. She sighs: “As a parent, you always tell your kids that education is the key. But if the school itself shuts the door, what are we supposed to tell them?”
Le groupe se tait un instant, puis Malik: The group falls silent for a moment, then Malik breaks the silence: “We do what we can. We work, we survive. But it feels like we’re waiting for a real chance to make it.” Joey nods. “Even if I wanted to go back to school, it’s not that simple. I have rent to pay. I can’t just stop working.”
Hana hausse les épaules. « Parfois, j’ai: Hana shrugs. “Sometimes I feel like going back too. But I’m scared they’ll still look at me the way they did before. Like I was already a lost cause.”
Le McDonald’s commence à se vider. Fatou: The McDonald’s is starting to empty out. Fatou gives me one last look before leaving. “My son is not a lost cause. None of these young people is. But they need us to look at them differently.”
Malik, Joey et Hana terminent leurs bois: Malik, Joey and Hana finish their drinks. Tomorrow, they’ll go back to their routine. Some may find a way back to school. Others will keep looking for alternatives.
Et le système, lui, continuera d’avancer: And the system will keep moving forward, often without them…
Comme eux, des centaines de jeunes dispa: Like them, hundreds of young people vanish from Montréal’s school radar every year. They leave school without a diploma, pushed out by a system that seems to have forgotten them.
Selon l’Institut de la statistique du Qu: According to the Institut de la statistique du Québec, from 2022 to 2023, 15% of Quebec students dropped out before earning their diploma. That figure, however, masks much higher dropout rates, particularly in disadvantaged neighbourhoods such as Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Saint-Michel and Montréal-Nord. In these neighbourhoods, nearly one student in five leaves school. They are young people too often from recent immigrant backgrounds, racialized or marked by poverty, who end up believing they matter to no one.
Notons aussi que les garçons décrochent: It should also be noted that boys drop out more than girls (18% versus 12.3%) and that leaving school is correlated with a fragile economic situation, according to data from Quebec’s Ministry of Education. Moreover, in Montréal, some drop out because they are tired of fighting alone. Others because no one comes looking for them when they disappear from the attendance lists.
<strong>« Si tu décroches, personne n’ir: “If you drop out, no one will come looking for you”
C’est ce qui a failli arriver à Malia. J: That’s what almost happened to Malia. I meet her outside École secondaire Eulalie-Durocher. That Thursday, the sky is grey and the air heavy with end-of-day fatigue. Groups of students slowly file out of class. Some are in a hurry to get home, others linger at the entrance, finishing their conversations. The school, located in the Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve borough, is a refuge for those seeking a second chance, a last stop before dropping out completely.
Un sac sur l’épaule et des écouteurs aut: A bag on her shoulder and headphones around her neck, Malia is 19. Of South African origin, she grew up here, in Hochelaga, where she still lives with her family. She agrees to talk to me. She is hesitant at first, then more and more at ease as the conversation goes on. “I almost dropped out so many times!” she says with a nervous smile. “In regular high school, I was lost. I had teachers who didn’t even know me, and when I had problems, no one was there for me.”
Elle marque une pause, regarde les autre: She pauses, watching the other students leave one by one. “My mother always told me school was important. But how do you stay motivated when (...) you feel like you can’t keep up with everyone else?”
Malia scratches her head, looking thoughtful. “In Secondary 5, I let go. I stopped coming. I had lousy jobs, I stayed out late, I told myself: ‘What’s the point?’ No one in my family had gone far in school, so it was easy to just give up.”
Son regard se durcit. « Mais un jour, un: Her gaze hardens. “But one day, a teacher noticed, more than once, that I was leaving his class in the middle of it. At the start of one of his classes, he took me aside and said something to me that stuck with me: ‘You know, Malia, if you drop out, no one here will come looking for you. But if you stay, we’ll fight with you.’”
Elle rit doucement. « Ça m’a vraiment fa: She laughs softly. “It really did something to me. No one had ever talked to me like that.”
Après une longue discussion avec ce prof: After a long talk with that teacher, Malia decided to come back, but differently. “I came here, to Eulalie, because it’s not like regular high school. Here, you’re with other adults, there’s less judgment. We’re here to learn, but at our own pace.”
Elle pointe du menton un petit groupe d’: She nods toward a small group of friends laughing a little further away. “There’s real support between us. When I’m struggling with something, there’s always someone to help me. I never had that before.”
Malia checks the time on her phone. She has to go, but before she does, she adds: “I want to finish high school and go do a DEP. I found something that motivates me: special education. Before, I never would have thought I’d have a plan like that. Now, I really want to make it.”
Elle me regarde et sourit. « Il y a plei: She looks at me and smiles. “There are plenty of young people like me who leave school because they feel alone in the system. But here, I understood that sometimes, just one person who believes in you can change everything.”
Elle rajuste son sac, me serre la main e: She adjusts her bag, shakes my hand and walks off down the street, soon disappearing among other students.
Pour comprendre ce qui pousse les jeunes: To understand what pushes young people to drop out, I spoke with Nassera Éloire, coordinator of Revdec, a Montréal community organization that has been fighting school dropout for 40 years. At her side was Cyril Guiot, a psychosocial worker. The organization, located in Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, welcomes about forty young dropouts, or youth at risk of becoming dropouts, aged 12 to 16, each year.
Il fait beau ce jour-là, mais l’air est: It’s a beautiful day, but the air is still cool for early spring. I arrive at Revdec’s offices, and Nassera greets me. She hands me a cup of hot coffee and sets me up in her office. A few minutes later, Cyril joins us. He has a contagious smile. He sits down in turn, and the conversation continues among the three of us.
Revdec, expliquent-ils, c’est une initia: Revdec, they explain, is an initiative that was born in the 1980s. It was championed by Michel Jacques, a member of the Brothers of the Christian Schools and an educator committed to Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, who has since died. He wanted to give young people a place where they could “take charge of their lives and flourish by focusing on their strengths.” But the name of the organization was chosen by the first young people who were welcomed there.
« Ils disaient que RevDec, c’était un rê: “They said Revdec was a dream for dropouts,” says Nassera.
Nassera Éloire, la coordonatrice de Rev: Nassera Éloire, coordinator of Rev Dec.
Un rêve, oui. Mais surtout une réponse à: A dream, yes. But above all a response to what the system doesn’t see. Because for those who walk through Revdec’s doors, dropping out didn’t begin with report cards.
« Ce n’est jamais l’école, la vraie rais: “It’s never school, the real reason,” Nassera says with certainty. “It’s never academic. The academic problem is a consequence. At the root, it’s something else: social anxiety, bullying, trauma, missing diagnoses. If the young person isn’t well with themselves, it can’t work at school.”
Cyril évoque aussi un facteur souvent né: Cyril also points to an often overlooked factor: the effects of social media on self-perception. “For some young people, what they see on their phone is reality. They think everyone sees the same thing they do. That what’s circulating is the absolute truth.” The result: comparison becomes constant, and the image they have of themselves can collapse at the slightest comment or look online.
À Revdec, les jeunes ne sont pas traités: At Revdec, young people are not treated as cases to be fixed, but as people to be listened to. Nassera describes the organization as a “break from school,” a complete alternative designed to give breathing room and structure back to young people who have lost their footing. Two kinds of paths are offered: a short-term program lasting a few weeks, and a long-term one that can last an entire school year, depending on need.
Ils viennent quatre jours par semaine. L: They come four days a week. In the morning, they study certain school subjects, sent by their home school. In the afternoon, there are workshops: sports, arts, discussions, prevention. And above all, every week, a personalized psychosocial follow-up is carried out.
« Un jeune qui a du mal à arriver à l’he: “A young person who has trouble arriving on time, we don’t punish them,” Cyril says. “We understand that it’s their challenge, and we build around that. There’s no single path here, just adapted ones.” Some young people say it themselves: here, for the first time, they don’t feel judged. “It feels like I’m allowed to be me,” one of them told the team.
<strong>Un organisme accessible, un syst: An accessible organization, a system slow to react
Malgré tout ce qu’offre Revdec, il ne pe: For all that Revdec offers, it cannot make up for the flaws of the school system on its own. The organization remains modest in size, and its capacity is limited by its resources.
Nassera me regarde en souriant et me dit: Nassera looks at me, smiling, and says, almost fatalistically: “We’re small, Revdec. Compared to the number of high school students in Montréal, it’s nothing.”
Revdec reste pourtant accessible à quico: Yet Revdec remains accessible to anyone who asks: the young people themselves, their parents, schools or even the DPJ. All it takes is to be enrolled in school and fill out a form, which is available on the organization’s website.
Les outils sont là. Ce qui manque, c’est: The tools are there. What’s missing is the signal, which has to be sent at the right time. “Even when a young person is no longer going to school, it sometimes takes several months before a parent, a school, a social service calls us,” she laments.
Le temps que l’école constate son absenc: By the time the school notices the prolonged absence, a report is made to the DPJ, and then the intervention takes place, the thread between the young person and school may already have snapped.
À cela s’ajoute une instabilité financiè: On top of that, there is financial instability weighing on the team. “We’re lucky to have a grant, mainly from the Ministry of Education, but it isn’t recurring. We have to rework it every year. And if we’re always obliged to create new projects to get funding, we can’t focus on our mission.”
<strong>Changer les règles, pas les jeun: Changing the rules, not the young people
Mais malgré les obstacles, ils gardent f: But despite the obstacles, they keep faith in what can be changed.
Nassera parle d’une école à repenser : p: Nassera talks about a school that needs to be rethought: more attentive to individual needs, more flexible in its paths, more human. “If a young person needs four or five years to complete their first cycle, that’s fine. What matters is that they get there.”
Elle insiste aussi sur ce qui semble fai: She also insists on what seems to make all the difference: relationship. “What helps is someone who stays there. Even when the young person pulls away. Someone who doesn’t let go.”
Autre point qu’elle juge essentiel : les: Another point she considers essential: overly rigid rules that block the momentum of many young people. She gives the example of those who, despite being totally or almost totally absent from class, move from one year to the next, until they find themselves blocked at the entrance to Secondary 3 because they never validated their first cycle. Add to that programs that are inaccessible depending on age, forced moves from one cycle to the next, and response times in the school system that are far too long.
Toutes ces barrières administratives, mi: All these administrative barriers, taken together, close doors on young people who simply needed a little more time or a few adjustments.
Avant que je parte, Nassera me confie un: Before I leave, Nassera shares one last thought with me. A message she often gives to the young people she works with: “What matters is that they keep hope in themselves, that they have confidence, that they manage to be happy and fulfilled. That’s what we want for them, even more than a diploma. Just that they stay positive.”
Chaque jeune rencontré, chaque intervena: Every young person I met, every worker I heard from, recalls one simple thing: dropping out doesn’t happen only at school. It happens in the way we look, or fail to look, at young people, at those who fade away. And if organizations like Revdec manage to bring them back, it’s because they don’t wait for them to be “fixed” before welcoming them.
Le décrochage scolaire est souvent perçu: Dropping out is often seen as an individual defeat. But for those who have lived it, it isn’t necessarily giving up. It’s an escape. Exhaustion. A way of saying that something is wrong. And sometimes, all it takes is a place where someone is truly expecting you for the momentum to return.
Il y a tant de jeunes qu’on laisse parti: There are so many young people we let go without offering them a real alternative. Not all of them will be lucky enough to benefit from Revdec’s help. The people I met told me repeatedly that if the school system, institutions, decision-makers and even citizens allowed themselves to look at these young people differently, perhaps, collectively, we would stop losing them in silence.
